Taiwan-Based Hacker Used BOSSAI AI Agents to Steal Taipei Emergency Dispatch Records

# Taiwan-Based Hacker Used BOSSAI AI Agents to Steal Taipei Emergency Dispatch Records

 Swati Khandelwal  Nov 09, 2026 Artificial Intelligence / Cyber Espionage

A single attacker using AI agents pulled emergency dispatch records covering seven Taipei districts, researchers at Acronis's Threat Research Unit said last week.

The agents also found a Taipei fire department platform exposing patient data from 2018, including ECG readings and ambulance video footage, without a login.

The researchers are highly confident that the attacker is a single person based in Hualien City, Taiwan. He aimed the agents at hundreds of organizations in at least 11 countries, including emergency services, banks, universities and military systems. The agents collected data or accessed systems at about 10 of them in Taiwan, Mexico and Thailand.

The evidence comes from the attacker's own server, which initially appeared to be a misconfigured development system. It turned out to be his operational attack platform, containing more than 90,000 files, including the agents' conversations, his command history, hacking tools, credentials, and victims' data.

The agents did not communicate with each other, so the attacker manually pasted one agent's output into another. Commercial AI models mostly refused to help him attack. The attacking agents therefore ran almost entirely on "abliterated" models, meaning AI models run locally with their safety training removed.

# What the Agents Reached

Taiwan was targeted far more heavily than any other country, according to the researchers' technical analysis . The most serious confirmed harm there involved emergency-services data.

The dispatch records came from a city's system for 119, Taiwan's emergency number for fire and ambulance services. The agents pulled them from the system's API, and they include incident times, response types, case status, and street-level locations. They are case records, not live ambulance tracking.

The researchers' summary says breaches at emergency services and universities led to the theft of medical and personal data. Their detailed account of the Taipei patient platform, however, says only that the records were exposed.

The agents also went after five other targets tied to Taiwan's emergency services:

Target
What the agents did
Result

Fire-dispatch technology vendor
Logged into its database admin panel with default root credentials. A web shell attempt through a known CVE failed.
Access to 18 or more database tables

Emergency management information system
Found a hardcoded AES-256 key in the site's front-end JavaScript that exposed session-cookie contents, including an administrator's identity
No confirmed compromise

National disaster-response center
A scanning tool reported a critical Apache remote code execution flaw
The flaw did not exist

National fire agency single sign-on portal
Tried to guess logins (brute force)
No confirmed access

Fire-department systems in five cities
Scanned them to identify the software they run
No confirmed compromise

The report does not say whether the affected organizations or Taiwan's authorities were told, or whether the exposed data can still be reached.

Outside emergency services, the agents pulled data from an account table at a Taiwanese lending firm through SQL injection. In Thailand, they collected data from three universities in the same way, after selecting 489 potential targets across 45 institutions.

In Mexico, they collected about 206,800 home phone records containing names and addresses, using government statistics, postal code lists, and telecom authority data.

About 15 more organizations were attacked without a confirmed break-in. In at least eight other countries, targets were only scanned or lined up for attacks that had not run by the time the researchers looked.

The researchers watched the operation for 12 days. One recorded exchange shows the attacker at work on July 25.

# How the AI Was Used and Where It Failed

The setup, called BOSSAI, had 12 AI agents, with 9 in use. Some built and maintained the attacker's servers and tools, while others scanned targets and carried out attacks.

Commercial cloud models did most of the building, with Grok as the main builder. When the attacker directly asked them to attack, Grok and MiniMax M3 refused and requested written proof that the work was authorized. The researchers say it is unclear whether a fake authorization letter would have changed that.

Grok made one exception, repairing a broken proof-of-concept script that the attacker then handed to an attack agent. The attacker also redirected the coding agents Claude Code and Codex to an abliterated model, though they mostly did infrastructure work. Cursor, another coding agent, attacked a Taiwanese emergency-services site while running such a model.

The abliterated models were versions of DeepSeek, GLM, and Qwen.

The agents also got things wrong. One scanning tool invented CVEs, and more than half of its high and critical findings were false positives or wrongly classified. The main attack agent also reported results that had not happened.

# Who Ran It

Acronis's attribution rests on mistakes the attacker made while hiding his identity, combined with publicly available information. He reused a single id

Claude Code's “Don't Ask Again” File Exposes Passwords and Keys in 1,122 Public Copies on GitHub

# Claude Code's “Don't Ask Again” File Exposes Passwords and Keys in 1,122 Public Copies on GitHub

 Swati Khandelwal  Nov 07, 2026 Artificial Intelligence / Developer Security

Passwords and API keys that developers typed into commands they approved in Claude Code are sitting in public GitHub repositories, where anyone can read them.

When a user selects " Yes, and don't ask again ," Anthropic's AI coding assistant can save the command, word-for-word, including the secret, in a project settings file.

Software security company Apiiro said yesterday that 1,122 public copies of that file hold at least one secret, though it did not test whether any still work. One company the researchers notified earlier this week confirmed its key had been live.

The file is .claude/settings.local.json. Removing it from a project does not undo the leak, because older versions stay in git history and in forks of the repository. The researchers' advice is to rotate first: change every password, token, and key the file has ever held, then clean up.

# How a Secret Lands in the File

By default, Claude Code asks before it runs most shell commands. If the user picks "Yes, and don't ask again," it saves an allow rule in .claude/settings.local.json inside the project, according to its permissions documentation . Matching commands then run without asking in later sessions.

The rule covers only what the prompt offered. Sometimes that is a pattern, such as npm test *, and sometimes one exact command. When it is the exact command, any password or token typed into it is saved too, in plain text.

In public files, the researchers found saved commands with the secret still inside, and they reproduced the behavior with the latest models, Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1.

Claude Code tries to keep the file out of git. The first time it writes the file in a git repository, it adds the file to the user's global git excludes, its settings documentation says. Git on that computer then ignores the file in every repository.

That protection stays in one user's git settings on one computer. It does nothing for a file that was already committed, the researchers say. Claude Code never adds the file to the project's own .gitignore, so the protection does not travel with the project.

In 539 of the 1,105 repositories the researchers traced, a commit listing Claude as a co-author changed the file. They take this to mean Claude often commits the file itself.

# What Apiiro Found

Apiiro's search of public GitHub found 104,185 copies of the file in 103,617 repositories, its research write-up shows. About 1.1% of them, or 1,122 copies, hold at least one secret. Together they hold 1,379 different secrets.

A value counted as a secret when it matched a known key format, or when a password or token sat beside the address of a public server. An AI reviewer also had to agree. The researchers do not say whether anyone has used these secrets.

More than a third of the secrets open a database directly, including 379 database passwords. Others include 43 SSH logins for public servers, 42 tokens for GitHub, GitLab and npm, and 23 AWS keys.

Among the owners of these files are 63 organizations, mostly software companies of all sizes. The strongest cases include a database vendor's own admin-level cloud key and the owner password of a medical-records database, the researchers say.

As of Monday, every file with a secret was still on its repository's default branch, and in half of those repositories it had been there for at least 217 days.

Older versions of the file contain 734 more secrets across 509 repositories that are not present in any current copy, usually because the file was deleted. Forks spread the files further: 211 forks of 74 repositories carry the same secrets as the originals.

Secrets also sit in 298 of 76,011 copies of the shared .claude/settings.json file, which teams commit on purpose, mostly inside allow rules. Including those, the older versions, and saved agent chat logs, the total is 2,539 secrets across 1,994 repositories.

Of 16 coding agents whose documentation the researchers compared, Claude Code is the only one confirmed to save the full approved command in a project file by default.

# What to Do

For developers, the researchers recommend these steps:

- Search your GitHub organization for .claude/settings.local.json and .claude/settings.json, and check each repository's git history for them, even where the files are gone.

- Rotate every password, token and key the files have ever held, before cleaning up.

- Stop tracking the local file with git rm --cached .claude/settings.local.json, and add it to the repository's own .gitignore.

- Open the file on your own computer, even if it was never committed, and delete every rule that contains a secret.

- Keep secrets out of commands. Refer to them as variables from a secrets manager, such as $DB_URL, so the saved rule holds the variable name and not the secret.

- Approve patterns, such as Bash(npm run:*), instead of single commands.

Copies that never reach GitHub still matter, the researchers say. The file is plain JSON in the project folder, and it can also be left inside an npm package, a Docker image, a zip archive, or a synced folder.

results:
The search found no new CAC rule scheduled for November 2026. The main labelling regime is already in force, and enforcement is ongoing.

- **Base rules:** The Measures for Labelling AI-Generated and Synthetic Content, jointly issued by the CAC, MIIT, the Ministry of Public Security and the NRTA, took effect on 1 September 2025 together with the mandatory national standard GB 45438-2025. Under them, visible labels and embedded metadata are both required, and nobody may remove, alter or forge a label.
- **Platform and app duties:** App distribution platforms must verify whether apps offer AI generation services and review their labelling materials.
- **2026 enforcement:** In April 2026 the CAC directed local cyberspace authorities to take action against the Jianying and Maoxiang apps and the Jimeng AI website for labelling failures. A later round, dated 15 September 2026, reportedly ordered a generative AI mini program offline for missing explicit and implicit labels and for skipping security assessment.
- **Scope:** Sources differ on whether ordinary users are covered. One says platforms must flag content they suspect is AI-generated, and users must declare AI content when they publish it.

Caveats: these are mostly secondary compliance-firm and tracker sites, several with inconsistent dates. I did not find a primary CAC document or any announcement tied to November 2026, so verify against cac.gov.cn before relying on any specific date.

# Former OpenAI Engineer Pleads Not Guilty to Planting Covert Device in Executive Meeting Room

 Ravie Lakshmanan  Nov 09, 2026 Cyber Espionage / Insider Threat

The OpenAI engineer who was arrested and charged last month for planting a covert audio recording device in the company's office has pleaded not guilty.

According to reports from Bloomberg and CNBC , Saudi national Abdulrahman Alfozan made an appearance in San Francisco federal court on Friday, where he entered the plea. His next hearing is scheduled for November 17, 2026.

If proven guilty, the 35-year-old faces a maximum of five years in prison and a $250,000 fine, followed by three years of supervised release. He has been held without bail since his arrest on October 9, 2026.

Late last month, a grand jury indicted Alfozan on a single count of interception of oral communications.

Prosecutors allege that the former OpenAI employee placed a "sophisticated recording device" in an executive OpenAI conference room in what has been described as an attempt to unlawfully record sensitive conversations.

He was arrested three days before he, along with his wife and son, were scheduled to fly from San Francisco to Riyadh on a one-way ticket.

"His wife and son, however, immediately left the United States without him," U.S. prosecutors said. "Rather than wait until the October 12 flight as booked, they initially planned to fly to Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, on October 11 on a one-way ticket booked and paid for by the Saudi government."

"That flight was canceled, however, when a member of the Saudi military booked and paid for yet another one-way ticket for the defendant's wife and son, this one business class to Doha, Qatar, on October 10, 2026. They did make that flight, departing San Francisco about 36 hours after the defendant was arrested."

In a subsequent court filing, it was alleged that Alfozan was in frequent contact with a member of the Saudi Royal Family via WhatsApp. He was also deemed a flight risk, with court documents claiming that the defendant took great pains to create bespoke, encrypted recording devices to record sensitive meetings involving senior OpenAI personnel and executives.

{"stdout":"### 2611.09822v1 | Discovering formally verified quantum programs with AI
AUTHORS: Sergey Shirobokov, Ben Jaderberg, Katerina Hristova, George Tsoukalas, Johannes Bausch, Eric Wieser, Francisco J. H. Heras, Nicholas C. Rubin, Guang Hao Low, Sébastien Racanière, Nenad Tomašev, Lei M. Zhang (+13)
ABS: The timeline by which quantum computers can solve breakthrough problems in science depends on improved quantum algorithms as much as on better hardware. Such algorithmic advances are typically achieved through many years of expert human collaboration. In mathematics and computer science, large language models have accelerated progress through automated discovery loops. However, quantum algorithms can only be evaluated by classical computers on restricted or small instances. Here we demonstrate automated discovery of quantum programs beyond these regimes including order-of-magnitude improvements on scientific applications. To achieve this, we build a quantum program library in the Lean theorem prover in which large language model agents synthesize novel programs against formal problem specifications and verify their correctness and cost. Agent teams collaborate, sharing results and knowledge through wikis and discussing ideas at organized conferences. Our results improve on prior baselines for parallel search (up to 1.4x), quantum arithmetic (290x), and simulations relevant to fusion, photochemistry and drug-metabolism by 11x, 8x and 2.5x respectively. Combining human and artificial intelligence at scale, under the rigor of mathematical proof, lets researchers design algorithms that today's classical and quantum computers cannot test, shortening the path to practical quantum computation.

### 2611.09892v1 | On Agentic Manipulation Policies
AUTHORS: Chen Chen, Omid Bagherieh, Naveen Nikamanth Appiah Balaji, Jesse T. Gonzalez, Negin Heravi, Fahad Islam, Xueting Li, Jean-Baptiste Regli, Kejia Ren, Petr Švec, David J. Yoon, Matthias Müller (+1)
COMMENT: Videos and code available at: https://apple-aiml-research.github.io/ml-amp/
ABS: Recent work on robot manipulation has focused on specialist policies trained on demonstrations. We show that generalist AI models can control manipulators more reliably than specialist policies such as vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs). We systematically analyze agentic manipulation policies (AMPs), in which a generalist AI model commands the manipulator directly, adapting its actions as the task unfolds. We present AMP1, a reference harness that runs unchanged across single-arm, bimanual, and mobile manipulation. AMP1 achieves state-of-the-art results on the RoboLab-120 and CaP-Gym benchmarks, with no demonstrations or task-specific training. On RoboLab-120, AMP1 reaches an 85.6\% success rate zero-shot, compared to 49.2\% and 42.9\% for leading VLA and WAM policies. The agent succeeds zero-shot in 104 of 108 real-world trials spanning twelve tasks and three robot instances, reducing failure rates by 20x and 15x relative to strong VLA and WAM baselines. The basic harness supplies no grasping, pushing, or placing skills; the agent develops its own strategies, such as searching for hidden objects, using objects as tools, and calibrating its cameras. With the addition of a persistent memory store, the agent can also learn from experience: an augmented harness with a memory representation that is carried across episodes lowers the failure rate on RoboDojo bimanual manipulation tasks by 4.6x relative to zero-shot deployment. Our analysis suggests that AMPs are substantially more general and robust than specialist manipulation policies, providing a promising foundation for robot manipulation.

### 2611.09798v1 | Test-Time Compute Scales Better with Parallel Agent Teams
AUTHORS: Junlin Wang, Haozhe Chen, Ang Li, Rahul Chalamala, Zhuang Liu 
COMMENT: 29 pages, 18 figures, 4 tables. Code: https://github.com/modal-projects/parallel-agent-teams-scaling
ABS: Test-time scaling improves the performance of a fixed model by spending more computation at inference. There are two common ways to spend it on agents when a verifier can score every attempt. Best-of-N sampling runs many independent agents and keeps the best result but saturates quickly. One large team of collaborating agents can score higher but stops improving as it grows. Can we get the best of both? Our method, parallel agent teams, does so by sampling many small teams in parallel and keeping the best team's result. We test it on 12 long-horizon tasks from GPU kernels and formal proofs to exploit development. With a 27B model and a budget of 100 agents, parallel teams of ten beat parallel agents on 10 of 12 tasks and beat one team of 100 on all four tasks where we ran such large teams. At equal dollar cost the same parallel teams beat a frontier model on half the tasks. A simple statistical model shows that individual agents lose because their many samples have a low mean and that one large team loses because a single sample gets no gain from variance. Sampling many small teams in parallel balances a high mean with the gain from variance. Parallel agent teams thus offer a more effective way to scale test-time compute.

### 2611.09729v1 | One Run Is Not Enough: A Monte Carlo Protocol for Evaluating LLM Reliability on Data Science Tasks
AUTHORS: Wenqi Ni, Ozan Evkaya, Miguel de Carvalho 
ABS: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise for automating data science workflows. Benchmarks such as DataSciBench (2026) and StatQA (2024) have advanced the evaluation of their capabilities across data science and statistical tasks. Assessing their reliability requires examining both the quality of their responses and their consistency across repeated runs, task types, and difficulty levels. With this aim, we introduce DS-QA, a benchmark comprising 100 data science and statistics questions drawn from UK university courses, spanning 16 datasets and three difficulty levels. We develop a three-layer evaluation framework that combines general response properties (runtime, verbosity and text similarity), coarse-grained metrics (accuracy, code executability and completeness), and task-specific metrics. We evaluate OpenAI models using a Monte Carlo protocol with 100 repeated runs. The results reveal substantial variability in responses to data visualisation and supervised learning tasks, particularly at medium and hard difficulty levels, highlighting the importance of evaluating consistency alongside response quality. We also find that an increase of 0.1 in the word verbosity ratio corresponds to an increase of about 0.013 in the token verbosity ratio.

### 2611.09759v1 | A Tight Hierarchy for Chain of Thought
AUTHORS: Thanh Le, A. Pavan, N. V. Vinodchandran 
ABS: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning has emerged as a powerful paradigm for extending the computational capabilities of transformer-based models. A growing body of recent work has begun to uncover the fine-grained computational power of transformers augmented with CoT, as well as their connections to classical complexity theory. In this work, we advance this line of research by establishing the first hierarchy theorem for CoT-based computation. Our main result shows that for any reasonable resource bound $r(n) \geq n$ and any $\varepsilon > 0$, \[ \mathrm{CoT}(r(n)) \subsetneq \mathrm{CoT}(r(n)^{1+\varepsilon}), \] where $\mathrm{CoT}(r(n))$ denotes the class of decision problems solvable by transformers using $O(r(n))$ CoT reasoning steps on inputs of length $n$. Our result shows that increasing the number of CoT reasoning steps provably yields strictly greater computational power, establishing CoT steps as a fundamental resource in transformer-based computation. Unlike classical hierarchy theorems, which are typically proved via diagonalization, our approach leverages known coarse-grained simulations between CoT-augmented transformers and Turing machines in both directions. Building on these connections, we adapt the classical padding technique from complexity theory to this setting to obtain a tight hierarchy. A key technical contribution of our work is the implementation of padding within the transformer-based CoT model.

### 2611.09847v1 | Computer-Use Agents Are Embodied Generalists
AUTHORS: Pranjal Aggarwal, Sean Welleck 
COMMENT: 14 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables
ABS: In many areas of AI, general-purpose models have increasingly replaced handcrafted methods and specialized architectures. We argue that embodied AI is poised for a similar shift. Our key claim is that embodied tasks can be formulated as interaction with digital software. Specifically, we build software that renders an agent's view of a physical environment on a screen and provides controls for acting in it. A computer-use agent (CUA) can then perform embodied tasks through the same screenshots and keyboard and mouse actions that it uses to operate ordinary software. Using a single CUA design and changing only the software, our entries win first-, second-, third-, and sixth-place prizes across four ECCV workshop competitions, without any competition-specific agent tuning. These results suggest that the skills CUAs learn on software, such as visual grounding, precise clicking, and exploration, already carry over to embodied tasks, giving CUAs a far broader scope in embodied AI than previously realized. We therefore advocate that computer-use agents can be embodied generalists. Further, we advocate that, by following the training strategy that made computer-use agents general, embodied AI can converge on a single general model as well, ushering in a new era of general embodied AI. Website: https://pranjal2041.github.io/cua-embodied

### 2611.09780v1 | Strategic Competition and Convergence in LLM Leaderboards
AUTHORS: Naveen Raman, Fei Fang, Yiling Chen 
ABS: Leaderboards are a popular way to compare large language model (LLM) capabilities and can influence how model developers invest resources. We ask when competition on leaderboards leads developers to produce models with similar capability profiles, which we call monoculture, or similar performance levels. We study this by formulating leaderboard competition as a game in which model developers invest resources across capabilities to maximize their win rate. We show that similar production functions can induce similar capability profiles, while comparative advantage can sustain distinct capability profiles. We then study convergence in performance levels and show that diminishing returns can lead to an increasingly crowded competitive frontier. Using data from LM Arena and OpenRouter, we find that developers improve more in categories where they lag competitors, while still retaining category-specific advantages. At the same time, we find that the frontier of models becomes increasingly crowded, alongside increasingly diversified model usage patterns. Our results suggest that increasing competition does not need to produce interchangeable models, but can instead sustain competitive models with distinct strengths.

### 2611.09721v1 | MemoryDojo: Benchmarking Poisoning Through LLM Agent Memory
AUTHORS: David H. Yang, Blake Bullwinkel, Amanda Minnich, Mohammad Mohammadi Amiri, Giorgio Severi 
ABS: LLM agents benefit from using memory systems to improve performance on long-horizon, multi-session tasks. However, memory introduces a critical attack surface. Malicious instructions encountered in one session may be stored and propagated through memory before being retrieved and acted upon in later sessions. Because memory systems differ in how they process and retrieve information, the downstream effects of poisoning can vary significantly across systems. To quantify the effects of poisoning across different memory architectures, we introduce MemoryDojo, a benchmark for tracing the lifecycle of poisoned information through agent memory and measuring its influence on subsequent agent behavior. MemoryDojo is easily extensible, consists of 155 multi-session long-horizon trajectories covering four domains, and supports five different memory systems. Through our evaluation, we find that all memory systems are susceptible to memory poisoning, with substantial variation in downstream effects. We further propose a memory-aware poison optimization process that increases the poisoning efficacy, highlighting differences between memory architectures. AUTHORS: Tural Mehtiyev, Biruk Tadesse, Lawrence Arkoh, Wesley Assunção 
COMMENT: 11 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables. Replication package: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23992004
ABS: LLM-based coding agents such as Claude Code are guided by repository instruction files (also called context files or agent configuration files) like AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md, which are read in every agent session. As any documentation artifact, these files can fall behind the code and become stale (e.g., a test folder moves, but the file still points to the old one). In technical debt terms, such a stale instruction is documentation debt, and its interest is the cost it adds to every later agent session. Evaluations that check only task success can miss this cost, and the stale file can persist. In this study, we ask what leads agents to act on a stale instruction, how it affects their behavior and at what cost, and how they recover. We study three real-world stale instructions from active open-source repositories in depth, each a different kind of guidance: a test command, a code location, and a procedure for adding a component. Agents fix 22 maintenance tasks under three versions of each instruction (left stale, corrected to the current path, and removed), with the code and the task held fixed, and we analyze 732 trajectories of two models at the level of individual tool calls. We find that agents follow stale guidance when it is relevant to their tasks, sometimes even when correct information is available elsewhere. On the stale test command, Claude Sonnet 5.5 needed about tw

### 2611.09792v1 | Knowing When to Intervene: Causal Evaluation of AI Agents
AUTHORS: Ayush Sawarni, Wenqian Xing, Tijana Zrnic, Ramesh Johari, Vasilis Syrgkanis 
ABS: Current evaluations of agentic AI systems primarily rely on benchmarks. However, the static nature of benchmarks makes them uninformative about the value of auditing interventions at deployment time. For reliable deployment, we often need to determine within an agent's trajectory whether or not to intervene, e.g., by verifying the agent's current output or steering it toward different behavior, using either human review or more costly models or time-consuming agentic supervision. The value of such interventions is fundamentally a causal inference question, asking whether the causal effect of such an intervention is beneficial for the final outcome. Estimating this causal effect is particularly challenging due to the dynamic nature of the problem: the impact of an intervention depends on the current context and environment, as well as the agent's future behavior. We develop the first methodologically grounded framework for evaluating the causal effects of randomized interventions within agent trajectories. By leveraging a relatively small dataset of agent trajectories collected under randomized interventions such as verification or screening, we can estimate the dynamic causal effect of a rich class of (contextual) intervention policies. The structural parameters that we estimate can also be used to construct safety leaderboards that capture the risk of various agentic actions, 

### 2611.09472v1 | ENGRAM: From Agent Experience to Weights through Verified Consolidation
AUTHORS: Ruiyi Yang, Zechen Li, Lihuan Li, Du Yin, Hao Xue, Flora D. Salim 
COMMENT: 22 pages, 4 figures
ABS: Language-model agents use experience through external retrieval and parameter learning. Consolidating stored experience into model weights requires deciding both which experience to train on and when its external records can leave retrieval. Admission based solely on student mastery can exclude useful teacher demonstrations, while removal immediately after training can discard guidance that the model still needs. We introduce ENGRAM, a framework that separates training admission from memory release. A demonstration-aware gate admits skills based on student mastery or sufficient successful teacher demonstrations. The student learns from selected action traces with context from an Engram Trace Graph (ETG). A verification gate then compares the updated model without episodic retrieval against the base model with retrieval on reserved probes. Release requires valid training participation and scores meeting both relative and absolute criteria; records for skills that fail verification remain retrievable. Experiments across interactive and reasoning benchmarks show consistent gains over frozen-weight ETG controls, with ablations supporting demonstration-aware admission and selective adapter activation. A controlled held-out comparison shows that verified release substantially reduces the retrievable footprint while remaining close to retain-all performance and outperforming immediate

### 2611.09457v1 | Definitions, Label Names, or Demonstrations? Auditing What Governs LLM Annotation
AUTHORS: Viraj Mishra, Shubham Gupta, Dhruv Gupta, Yuehong Cassandra Tai, Qunhua Li 
ABS: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to annotate social-science texts, but high accuracy does not establish that they apply researcher-supplied category definitions: predictions may instead reflect prior associations with category labels or labeled demonstrations. We introduce a counterfactual audit that reassigns definitions among output labels, distinguishing adherence to supplied definitions from preservation of a dataset's original mapping. Across three political-text datasets, models rarely follow reassigned definitions, and standard fine-tuning strengthens the original mapping without reliably increasing definition adherence. We then study retrieval-augmented annotation. Retrieving the nearest training examples generally outperforms retrieving examples separately within each category despite using fewer demonstrations. On the two tasks with substantial gains, direct \(k\)-nearest-neighbor classification recovers 74--93\% of the improvement, indicating that neighborhood labels provide much of the predictive signal. Relabeling fixed demonstrations redirects predictions, whereas aligning demonstrations with reassigned definitions substantially increases adherence to the new mapping. ### 2611.09454v1 | From LoRA to Language: Recovering Skill Documents from Adapters
AUTHORS: Saranya Dintakurthy Swadha, Pavan C Shekar, Arpit Jain, Aswanth Krishnan 
COMMENT: 29 pages, 5 figures, 18 tables
ABS: Agent skills are short documents that teach a language model how to handle a class of tasks. To save context, these documents are increasingly compiled into low-rank adapters (LoRA), which keep the behaviour but lose the text: an adapter is hard to read, edit, audit or move to another model. We ask whether the skill document can be written back from the adapter and its frozen base model, and we score each recovered document by the share of the original's key instructions it states and by the tasks it solves. Reading the weights alone recovered little with the methods we tried; a learned map from weights to text passed on about one bit of the document. Running the adapter worked much better. The Executing Writer, a small writer trained on top of the adapted model, recovers 39-44% of the key instructions of held-out skills, against 1.3-1.5% with another skill's adapter, and on adapters fitted to 41 external skills its documents restore 85-91% of the original's task gain. These strongest results are on adapters whose training stored the document; adapters trained on behaviour alone are much harder for trained writers (1-2% of instructions). For these adapters we test an agent that runs the base and adapted models and writes a skill from where they differ. On ALFWorld its skills recover 58-71% of a LoRA's gain and carry over to models that cannot load the LoRA, lifting Llama-3.1-8B

### 2611.09446v1 | Logit Laundering: Evading Data-Use Auditing in Large Language Models
AUTHORS: Ruihan Hu, Wei Luo, Yu-Ming Shang, Jiakai Wang, Chuxuan Zhang, Mei Li, Xi Zhang, Meikang Qiu 
COMMENT: Accepted to ACM CCS 2026
ABS: Data-use auditing in Large Language Models (LLMs) aims to determine whether the given data has been used for training, thereby supporting data ownership safeguards. A dominant solution is data watermarking, which embeds traceable signals into training data and detects them in model outputs. Recent studies have proposed many watermarking-based auditing methods in LLMs. However, systematic investigation from an adversarial perspective remains limited: non-compliant LLM providers would use unauthorized copyrighted datasets for training their own models to enhance model capabilities, while attempting to evade detection by auditors, thereby avoiding legal liability. To fill this research gap, we propose a novel evasion framework, termed Logit Laundering, where the non-compliant LLM provider manipulates model outputs at inference time to undermine detectable watermark signals. Specifically, we design a logit reshaping module to suppress watermark-induced statistical signals by integrating a statistical bias estimator as a plug-and-play component. This design keeps the model parameters unchanged and performs manipulation only in the logit space, thereby enabling auditing evasion while minimizing the impact on model's learned knowledge. To further balance evasion effectiveness and model utility, we introduce a confidence-aware scaling module to adaptively calibrate the suppression stre

### 2611.09568v1 | Alignment by Confident Debate: Preference Learning from Multi-Agent Debate
AUTHORS: Nikhil Verma, Dingxian Wang, Mohammad Reza Rezaei, Andrew Rabinovich, Zhao Chen 
COMMENT: 53 pages, 9 Figures, 31 Tables
ABS: Post-training language models for reasoning typically rely on gold answers, task-specific verifiers, or learned reward models, limiting scalability when such signals are scarce. Multi-agent debate offers a self-supervised alternative, but converting debate into reliable training supervision remains challenging: majority voting weights agreeing responses equally, lacks a principled tie-breaking rule, and is ill-defined for open-ended tasks without a canonical answer; likelihood-based scoring can conflate fluency with correctness; and homogeneous committees may reinforce correlated errors. We introduce Alignment by Confident Debate (AbCD), which converts debate traces into preference data without gold answer labels. A sampling-diverse committee debates each problem, after which final answers are clustered by task-level semantic equivalence. We use verifiable tasks (mathematical reasoning, multiple-choice quantitative QA, and executable code-generation) as a controlled test bed: their answer keys or executable checkers let us evaluate the quality of debate-derived supervision against ground truth, even though the oracle itself never uses gold labels. Post-training on the resulting preferences outperforms inference-only ensembling and debate, as well as SFT on the same traces, across five model families spanning 1B to 8B parameters and four datasets, improving consensus accuracy, w

### 2611.09730v1 | What to Delegate, What to Preserve: Human Preferences for Agentic AI Across Everyday Life and Work
AUTHORS: Sarah Wheeler, Veronica Rammouz, Yaoyao Qian, Zexuan Liu, Mengyi Wei, Anthony Rios, Tianzhi He, Kyrie Zhou 
ABS: AI agents can execute multi-step tasks on users' behalf, yet the boundaries of acceptable delegation remain unclear. We report a scenario-based survey of 289 U.S. adults with prior AI experience covering 45 use cases across nine life domains. Each respondent evaluated one scenario per domain, producing repeated measures of automation preference, trust, collaboration, AI leadership, privacy concern, and willingness to pay. Automation preferences varied substantially across domains. Generalized estimating equation models showed that greater trust in the AI agent, desired AI leadership, prior task-specific AI use, and anticipated financial savings were associated with greater automation preference. In contrast, concerns that automation would reduce personal fulfillment predicted lower automation preference. Open-ended responses further revealed a preference for bounded autonomy, with participants often favoring substantial AI execution while retaining human involvement, oversight, or final authority. We argue that delegation is best understood as a configuration of execution, collaboration, leadership, and authority.

### 2611.09662v1 | How Much Conversation History Does an AI Agent Need?
AUTHORS: Danny Kim, Fernando Koch 
COMMENT: 10 pages, 6 figures
ABS: How does using less conversational history change reader-token use and benchmark scores? We examine this question on 1,100 BEAM questions. We held the retrieval ranking and reader constant across five fixed passage budgets, and mean assigned scores rose as the passage budget grew. The score gain per additional token became smaller at the upper tested budgets. Answerable questions generally received higher scores with more context. Pooled abstention scores sometimes rose as the passage budget shrank. We also tested message retention in a controlled task with explicit conversational-state targets and compared retained user messages with token-matched recency. Qwen matched the full state more often for direct requirements when user messages were retained. Its full-state matching declined when answers depended on references to earlier offers. Mistral produced near-floor results across the retention conditions. A scoring audit leaves the correctness of BEAM answers unresolved. These experiments characterize the token and score consequences of the tested memory budgets. Reliable budget selection depends on retaining the evidence each question requires and validating the measure used to assess answer quality.

### 2611.09573v1 | Half-precision inference of AI weather prediction models: negligible loss of skill at a fraction of the cost
AUTHORS: Stefan Siegert 
COMMENT: 40 pages, 15 figures, 9 tables. Code: https://github.com/sieste/ai-nwp-fp16
ABS: AI weather prediction models are released with 32-bit (fp32) weights and run in fp32 by default, although current GPUs compute much faster in 16-bit formats. We run five publicly available models -- Aurora, Pangu-Weather, FourCastNet, SFNO and FastNet -- on a single 16 GB GPU from 52 initial dates in 2024, in fp32 and with their networks in half precision (fp16), and verify the forecasts against ERA5. The physical state must stay in fp32: converting the whole model rounds it in physical units, which in fp16 overflows and in bf16 discards meaningful information. With the state, its normalisation and denormalisation in fp32, running the network in fp16 changes the global RMSE by at most 1.4%, and by about 0.5% or less for four of the five models, equivalent to less than one hour of lead time up to day 8 and at most two hours at day 10. The differences show no systematic pattern by region, scale or for tropical and extratropical storms, apart from a small tropical penalty in FourCastNet, and fp16 leaves the CRPS, spread and calibration of Aurora's ensemble almost unchanged. No value overflowed fp16's numeric range (+/-65,504); the largest stay 38 to 544 times below it. A 10-day forecast in fp16 is 1.3-3.5 times faster than in fp32 and uses 1.4-3.7 times less energy. results:
Recent coverage points to a mixed picture: AI is cited often in layoff announcements, but economy-wide job losses attributed to AI remain hard to pin down.

- **Challenger count:** A Challenger, Gray & Christmas report released November 6 tallied 121,401 AI-linked job-cut announcements in the first ten months of 2026. Weaker market and economic conditions have overtaken AI as the leading reason for layoffs, according to the same report.
- **Jobs report:** The October report showed the most AI-exposed sectors, information and finance, continued to struggle and have shed jobs on a trend basis, while professional and business services added 70,000 jobs in October.
- **Trackers:** Tallies differ by source. One tracker counts 88,164 jobs cut by 40 companies that blamed AI, 59,450 in 2026. Another says employers blamed artificial intelligence for 101,743 US job cuts in the first half. Notable recent cuts include Canva, which restructured 22% of its workforce, 1,271 people, on November 4.
- **Displaced workers:** A Goldman Sachs analysis found those workers were roughly 10 percentage points more likely to remain unemployed a year after losing their jobs. Since there is no definitive count of how many workers have lost jobs to AI, the figures are estimates.
- **Rehiring:** A SHL/Propeller survey found 19.1% of American respondents said they had personally been replaced by AI and were subsequently asked to return to their jobs. That survey is from June and July, and its sample is small.
- **Productivity:** An Atlanta Fed paper found nearly 90% of surveyed executives saw no measurable productivity or jobs change from AI.

I didn't find the official November 2026 BLS jobs report, so the employment figures above come from secondary coverage of the October data.

results:
The search didn't return any apiiro.com page, and none of the results mention Apiiro. The coverage I found is about Claude Code's `.claude/settings.local.json` file leaking secrets into published packages. Some reports attribute the research to Lakera and others to Check Point, so I can't confirm the Apiiro link.

- **The core issue:** When Claude wants to run a command it has not been permitted to run before, it presents you with options, one of which is "allow always". Choosing this writes the exact command string, to .claude/settings.local.json as a permanent allowlist entry.
- **Scale of the finding:** Across approximately 46,500 packages monitored over our scan window, 428 contained a .claude/settings.local.json. Of those, 33 files across 30 packages included credentials, meaning roughly one in thirteen exposed settings files contained sensitive data.
- **Why it slips through:** The settings file is a hidden dotfile that does not stand out in any part of the normal publish workflow. It's not gitignored by default.
- **Recommended response:** Rotate exposed tokens and check package contents before publishing. Lakera advises that npm tokens and GitHub tokens should be rotated, and using dry-run and unpack checks to verify that tarballs and other packages do not contain local assistant settings files is suggested.

Sources: Lakera's blog post (lakera.ai), coverage by IT Brief and SecurityBrief, and a Claude Code GitHub issue (claudeissues.com) that reports the same behavior. If you need the Apiiro piece specifically, a direct search on apiiro.com or its blog would be needed.

If you asked Claude Mythos one hundred thousand questions about cybersecurity, would learning the answers make you better at hacking? Would doing so make another AI model better at hacking? Using those questions and answers to train an AI model is a form of black-box distillation —a technique that improves a weaker “student” model by using a stronger “teacher” model’s outputs as a source for training. “Black-box” means the teacher model is closed-source, so it can only be prompted online using a web or software interface. Conversely, white-box distillation uses additional information about the teacher model’s internal processes, requires access to its weights, and is outside the scope of this explainer. 1

CEO-spoofing scammers used AI to help steal more than $100 million, feds say | The Record from Recorded Future News
Image: Benjamin R. via Unsplash

# CEO-spoofing scammers used AI to help steal more than $100 million, feds say
The Justice Department indicted three men for allegedly scamming companies out of more than $100 million with help from AI.
Jacob Soall, Sharon Hazan and Guy Sheetrit are accused of pretending to be company CEOs or lawyers and contacting lower-level employees to trick them into sending large payments to bank accounts they controlled.
Soall and Hazan were arrested in Spain this summer and Sheetrit was detained in the U.K. in September. The Justice Department said on Thursday that extradition requests for all three men are pending.
U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said the three used artificial intelligence “to impersonate real people and deceive corporate executives into sending them and their co-conspirators approximately $129 million.”
Hazan, 54, and Sheetrit, 42, are from Israel while Soall, 41, is Spanish. All three are facing up to 104 years in prison on multiple charges of money laundering, aggravated identity theft, wire fraud and more.
The men allegedly stole nearly $5 million from a hospital in Missouri, $2.6 million from a Rhode Island bank, $2.9 million from a hospital in California, $11.5 million from a tech company in the U.K., $4.6 million from a finance company in Massachusetts and $5.2 million from a Florida pet food company.
According to prosecutors, the conspiracy ran from 2024 to 2026 and involved the three as well as other co-conspirators deploying artificial intelligence as a way to spoof the voices and images of real corporate executives.
Court documents said several incidents involved the three men contacting employees and telling them they needed help with a confidential financial transaction, mimicking the CEO’s voice or image on the call.
To further the scheme, they would tell the employee to speak with lawyers at a large international firm that were working on the transaction — using AI to then make themselves look and sound like those lawyers.
The money was wired to accounts across the U.S., Europe, the UAE and China before the scammers transferred it to cryptocurrency.
Prosecutors said Soall typically impersonated the lawyers and had a script he used to mimic the attorneys. Hazan was in charge of laundering the funds, boasting in one instance of laundering $400 million since 1994, according to court documents. The Justice Department noted that Hazan was previously convicted of bank fraud in 2008.
Senior FBI official James Barnacle said criminals continue to weaponize emerging technology like artificial intelligence.
“The alleged scheme orchestrated by Soall, Hazan, and Sheetrit demonstrates how the use of advanced technology can be exploited to commit large scale fraud,” he said.
The FBI urged other companies that may have been victims to come forward.

The metro Detroit company that handles the rights to many of Eminem's best-known songs is suing the generative AI platform Suno, claiming the rapper's copyrighted music was used to train the model.
The lawsuit, filed late Friday night (Nov. 6) in San Francisco federal court, joins a growing flurry of litigation aimed at the AI song generator by music industry heavyweights.
The Ferndale-based publisher Eight Mile Style owns and administers the rights to nearly 270 Eminem compositions, including hits such as "Lose Yourself," "Without Me," "'Till I Collapse," "The Real Slim Shady" and "Stan." The publisher argues that Suno is benefiting "from the fruits of others' labor" and seeks more than $41 million in damages, claiming copyright infringement and other violations.

Eminem performs during the 37th Annual Rock & Roll Hall of Fame Induction Ceremony at Microsoft Theater on Nov. 5, 2022 in Los Angeles.

"The works are some of the most valuable in the world, and Eight Mile Style is very protective of these iconic songs," the lawsuit reads.
Advertisement

Advertisement

Advertisement

Advertisement

In Friday's filing, Eight Mile Style contends the Massachusetts-based Suno "has built their entire business model based on copyright infringement at a scale heretofore unseen."
Reached by the Detroit Free Press, a Suno spokesperson said Saturday: "Suno exists to help people create new, original music, not to trade on anyone's name or likeness, and we prohibit any unauthorized use of an artist's work. To protect against this, we do not allow prompts for specific artists' names and songs and work with third party providers to screen uploaded audio files and lyrics for potential misuse. We are always working to strengthen our guardrails and we will continue to add new safeguards that protect artists and our users."
Suno, which launched in 2023, allows users to generate songs with text and image prompts describing genres, styles, lyrical concepts and other elements. It offers free and paid subscription tiers.
In its 32-page complaint, the Eminem publisher notes that Suno has previously disclosed in court that its AI model was trained on "essentially all music files of reasonable quality that are accessible on the open Internet."
"Suno made illicit copies of millions of copyrighted musical works, including Eight Mile Style's works, and then – without any remuneration to the rights holders – created a platform where anyone capable of paying $10 per month can create complete songs based entirely on these illicit copies," the complaint reads.
Advertisement

Advertisement

Among the examples cited in the lawsuit is a Suno-generated track titled "Slim shady x Rosefalls," which uses an AI-generated image of Eminem as cover art and vocals "clearly derived from Eminem's actual voice," the publisher contends.
Other cited instances include verbatim or similar versions of lyrics from songs such as "Lose Yourself," "The Real Slim Shady" and "Houdini" in tracks generated by the service.
While Suno has implemented restrictions to block prompts that name specific artists – a user cannot type the cue "Eminem," for example – Eight Mile Style says those guardrails are easily bypassed.
For instance, the lawsuit says, users can prompt Suno to generate a "Slim Shady"-style track by using a string of terms such as "aggressive rap, rapid-fire flow, dark humor, male rapper, horrorcore, intense beat, bass-heavy, menacing, controversial."

A lawsuit filed by Eight Mile Style includes a screenshot attributed to the app HookGenius with descriptors of Eminem music.

Leaked Suno source code reportedly obtained by an online hacker shows that the AI service scraped Eminem music and lyrics from sites such as YouTube and Genius.com, the complaint notes.
Advertisement

Advertisement

Suno was sued in June 2024 by the Recording Industry Association of America on behalf of major record labels. Since then, two of those labels, BMG and Warner Music Group, have made licensing deals with the AI firm. Universal Music Group, Eminem's record company, remains a plaintiff.
Citing U.S. copyright law, Eight Mile Style lawsuit says it is entitled to $150,000 for each of the 269 Eminem songs it controls, or $40.4 million. The company also claims Suno illicitly removed digital copyright information embedded in the songs it trained on and is seeking an additional $672,000 in damages.

- **Who and what:** The defendants are Jacob Soall, 41, Sharon Hazan, 54, and Guy Sheetrit, 42. Hazan had a prior conviction: in 2008, he was convicted in a New York court of conspiracy to commit bank fraud. The worst of the patchpocalypse may be behind us, according to Linus Torvalds.
Writing in his weekly kernel update post , the Linux kernel dev leader delivered Linux 7.4 rc2 – the second rough cut of the next kernel – which he rated as a big release for two reasons.
One is that he left some code out of rc1, because he was busy and because it was already the largest such release in the history of the kernel.

REG AD

The other is what Torvalds described as “various AI fixes.”

REG AD

Such fixes are necessary because ever since Anthropic launched its Mythos bug-finding model in April , developers have been able to find more software flaws than was previously possible.
Microsoft, for example, addressed a record 974 flaws in September – its third record fixing spree this year after it whacked 622 flaws in July and 206 in June. Oracle addressed 1,449 flaws in a single month.
That’s many more patches than IT teams are set up to handle, yet they must find ways to deal with bugs more quickly because attackers are increasingly targeting flaws found by AI .
Torvalds’ post suggests that, perhaps, the worst of this is behind us.
“This time around Alexei claims that on the bpf side at least the fixes are now coming in faster than the new reports, and that sounds lovely if true,” he wrote.
That’s a reference to Alexei Starovoitov, co-creator and lead dev on the Extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF), the project that makes it possible to run sandboxed programs within the Linux kernel.
“I think most other areas haven't reached that point yet, but it's at least a sign that we _may_ be starting to see the tide starting to turn,” he added. “Don't hold your breath, but maybe cross your fingers we'll be getting there in the not entirely distant future.”
If Torvalds is correct, that’s welcome news. The Linux kernel’s 40-million-plus lines of code makes it one of the world’s bigger software projects. If AI soon stops finding flaws in other parts of the kernel beyond eBPF, perhaps the deluge of fixes developers and users alike will need to handle has peaked. ®

The Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act was introduced by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas). The sources disagree on the date. Most say it was introduced on September 23, 2026, and Democracy Now's September 24 headline describes it as unveiled on Wednesday. One outlet, political.org, says it was introduced on September 3. Sanders' office may have announced it on September 3 and formally introduced it later, but I can't confirm that from these results.

- **Ban:** The bill would permanently prohibit developing or deploying artificial superintelligence. It defines the term as AI that exceeds human cognitive performance across most domains, or has enough capability to destroy or disempower humanity, including by overthrowing the federal government.
- **Pause:** Advanced AI development would be paused temporarily until a federal regulator has set safety rules.
- **New agency:** The bill would create a cabinet-level Department of Artificial Intelligence to oversee advanced AI systems and enforce the bill's restrictions.
- **Penalties:** It would set penalties for people and entities that violate or circumvent its restrictions.
- **International:** Casar has said the bill pushes for international agreements so that no one, anywhere, builds AI too powerful for humans to control.

Most of the changes I make to my projects these days come in the form of PRs opened for me by Claude Code or Codex. The PR is my unit of work - I use them to bundle commits together, iterating on them until a feature is complete, document decisions and then merge the finished result. Today's coding agents are great at writing PR descriptions.

They're too good at describing the work

The problem is that they are too good. An agent-written PR description is accurate and comprehensive. It describes the problem, the detailed solution, and the steps taken to verify it. That's a lot of information to absorb.

It's not necessarily slop, but it reads like slop!

It's very easy to spot an AI-written PR, and as with other forms of AI writing my instant reaction is best summarized as "I'm not reading all of that". It doesn't matter how accurate or useful the information is, I'm instantly put off by the thought that it will take me longer to read than it took the driving author to write... even when that driving author is me!

I want human editorial judgement. I want someone to have thought just long enough about the PR to give me a human-approved introduction that helps me understand, at a high level, what the PR is for and whether it deserves more of my attention.

I think I've found a low-effort way to do this that feels right.

Hide most of it in a details/summary

The HTML <details><summary> elements render as a collapsed heading (the summary) t

This raises a practical question: when these modalities disagree, how can we detect and explain the conflict? We study this problem as modality-level inconsistency detection. We first introduce a taxonomy of cross-modal knowledge inconsistencies, covering information granularity differences, direct conflicts, temporal changes, and KG incompleteness. We then present Kontrast, an automatic framework that uses Text-to-SPARQL and LLM reasoning to compare table-based answers with KG evidence and categorize the resulting inconsistencies. Experiments on various Table-QA datasets show that cross-modal inconsistencies are common and informative. They reveal not only true knowledge conflicts, but also missing KG structure and temporal mismatches while being limited by Text-to-SPARQL errors and noise. Our analysis shows that text, tables, and KGs can complement and correct one another through systematic comparison. Kontrast provides a practical tool for large-scale knowledge auditing and establishes a benchmark for future work on cross-modal knowledge consistency. Code and data are available at this https URL . - **Performance:** In a head-to-head comparison within the 145-patient group, PREVIA flagged all 30 patients who later developed PTSD. A PTSD-specialist ED clinician caught 89% of them. NYU did not report its false-positive rate.

- **Design:** The tool runs several open-source models in layers. One model tends to emphasize risk signs, while another highlights protective factors. The first layer scans for symptoms during the initial trauma, like loss of control or amnesia, and early symptoms in the ED, such as feeling disconnected from the body.
- **Explainability:** Unlike many AI tools, PREVIA explains its reasoning and grounds predictions in established PTSD risk factors.
- **Context:** About 28% of emergency departments routinely screen for PTSD.

results:
Governor Hochul signed S9051-B on October 28, 2026, and it took effect as Chapter 368 of the Laws of 2026. The law adds Article 48 to the General Business Law (sections 1800 to 1805) and takes effect January 1, 2027.

- **Core prohibition:** Operators may not provide "unsafe AI companion features" to minors. Effective January 1, 2027, the law prohibits operators from providing "unsafe AI companion features" to minors in New York.
- **Covered technology:** The law applies to any "covered AI companion," defined as "a generative artificial intelligence system with a natural language interface, including via writing or sound, that provides ongoing, adaptive responses to user inputs."
- **Listed features:** Sources disagree on the count. One says the law prohibits operators of AI chatbots from offering minors a list of 12 "unsafe AI companion features", while another reports eleven unsafe AI companion features for minors. Examples include outputs that suggest the chatbot is human, that flatter the user or engage in sycophancy, or that encourage self-harm or secrecy.
- **Exclusions:** The prohibition does not apply where a companion is made available solely for (a) customer service or strictly providing information about commercial services or products or customer service account information, or (b) efficiency improvements or research or technical assistance, provided that the companion "is unable to respond on topics outside of the specified purpose"; or (c) a business entity's internal purposes or employee productivity.
- **Enforcement:** One source says the law gives enforcement to the Attorney General alone, and names no education exemption.
- **Sponsors:** Sponsored by Senator Kristen Gonzalez and Assemblymember Alex Bores through companion bill A10379C.

Sources were consistent on the signing date, chapter number, and effective date. The feature count (11 vs. 12) is the main discrepancy, so check the enacted text on legislation.nysenate.gov before relying on a specific number.

The search turned up one letter, and it is dated October 13, 2026, not November. Senators Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) and Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) sent it to National Intelligence Director Jay Clayton and OSTP Director Michael Kratsios. Some coverage describes the NIST center as CAISI and some as CAISSI, so the spelling varies by source.

- **Standards:** The letter asks NIST, including its center for advanced AI, to speed up technically grounded, measurable safety and security standards and risk-management frameworks. It also calls for working with industry on best practices, including secure testing environments and third-party data sharing.
- **Testing:** The senators want expanded independent evaluation of advanced models for national security risks. They also want work with industry, universities, state and local governments, and critical-infrastructure operators on defensive AI tools.
- **Context:** The letter follows Cantwell's six-point AI governance framework from early October. That framework calls for enforceable safety standards developed by NIST, and says covered models should not be released until an independent audit confirms they meet those standards. Cantwell did not give a timeline for the mandatory federal standards.

input.prompt: Date of article and original publisher. What did the White House finalize, when, what does it require, key numbers and quotes.

response.result:
**Source:** Originally published by the Daily Caller News Foundation (DCNF) on November 6, 2026. The page I reviewed is a repost on Economic Collapse Report, dated November 7, 2026, and credits Emily Kopp.

**What was finalized:** A White House policy that screens purchases of synthetic nucleic acids, the genetic materials scientists use in lab work. The White House Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP) announced it on a Thursday, through a letter from Director Michael Kratsios.

**Background and timing:** A May 5, 2025 executive order on gain-of-function research required this policy within 90 days. The article says it was published roughly 460 days after that deadline.

**What it requires:**
- Scientists receiving federal funding must buy synthetic nucleic acids from certified suppliers.
- Certified suppliers must ensure their customers are not bad actors or hostile foreign governments.
- The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) is expected to issue detailed standards and evaluation protocols within about 90 days.
- The Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) will then publish a list of certified suppliers.
- The government expects federally funded scientists to buy only from certified suppliers within a little over a year.
- The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) and HHS will examine whether certain dangerous genetic sequences should be added to the Federal Select Agent Program.

**Key context:**
- A 2024 Biden administration policy had a similar goal but no enforcement mechanism.
- The article notes that the U.S. is the leading supplier of synthetic nucleic acids to researchers worldwide.
- The Biosecurity Modernization and Innovation Act, pending in Congress, would extend screening to privately funded labs, regulate DNA printers, and consolidate gain-of-function rules.

**Quotes:**
- Kratsios described the policy as building "a dynamic biosecurity defense centered on strong controls" over materials used for synthetic biology misuse.
- Gerry Parker, a biodefense expert, said the policy "replaces an honor system with a real, verifiable system for accountability."

The article frames the policy as a response to fears of AI-enabled bioweapons, but the policy itself targets physical DNA supply chains rather than AI systems directly.

results:
The White House released a new National Policy for Nucleic Acid Synthesis Screening on November 5, 2026. Kratsios announced it on X, saying this policy establishes a new, government-wide screening requirements for synthetic DNA and the equipment used to make it. He also said NIST will issue rigorous new screening standards and HHS and USDA will certify synthetic biology providers.

The policy itself, which the search surfaced as a PDF on whitehouse.gov, is issued under Executive Order 14292. It replaces the 2024 Framework for Nucleic Acid Synthesis Screening and, on full implementation, the 2023 HHS Screening Framework Guidance. The excerpts I could see say federally funded customers must procure all synthetic nucleic acids from certified suppliers within 250 days. I could not confirm the full details of the certification process from the snippets.

For background, the 2024 framework relied on self-attestation. A July 2025 policy report criticized that approach, saying the previous administration's reliance on self-attestation of compliance by providers failed to close gaps in adherence to robust screening practices. The new policy's move to certification by named agencies appears to respond to that criticism.

Caveat: the search results did not include an official OSTP announcement page or the full text of the policy, so the details above come from the PDF excerpts and Kratsios's post. The full document on whitehouse.gov is the best source for the certification timeline and requirements.

response.stdout:
In that story The Times used the term “close relationship” to describe the Nvidia CEO's associations with both Ms Huang and US president Donald Trump.
On Sunday the newspaper alleged US authorities believe Alice Huang and Jensen Huang shared a "romantic" relationship.
The Times further alleges Ms Huang is a Chinese citizen who worked for a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed that has bought plenty of Nvidia hardware and is suspected of doing so to make it available to Chinese users, either by running inside datacenters or perhaps even facilitating transport to the Middle Kingdom.
The US has for years banned or restricted exports of advanced GPUs to China, partly because it feels Beijing’s armed forces can use them to build systems that will erode America’s military superiority.
Any relationship, of any sort, between Jensen Huang and a Chinese intelligence operative would therefore be enormously concerning. The company told the NYT that Jensen Huang and Alice Huang just had normal CEO-to-customer-exec chats that were no threat to Nvidia intellectual property or US national security.
Shortly after Nvidia’s board published its statement, Huang sent an email to staff that the company made public .
“I owe my family and all of you an apology,” the email opens. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”
Huang’s email doesn’t explicitly link his actions to The Times’ reports, but he says he supports the Nvidia board’s decision to open its investigation “and will cooperate fully.”
"To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me," he wrote, without specifying if that's a reference to infidelity. "Leading NVIDIA is the privilege of my life. My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence."

“I love our country and our company,” the CEO added. “I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American.”
The CEO’s mail, and the board’s statement, make no allegations about any “close relationship” with Ms. Huang.
The exact nature of that relationship therefore remains mysterious, as does Nvidia’s relationship with Singapore, a tiny island nation that has sometimes been the source of 22 percent of the company’s revenue.
Singapore is simply incapable of hosting as much Nvidia kit as that volume of purchases would buy, because its government limits datacenters to 1.6 GW of energy consumption. When asked to explain that oddity, Nvidia has said that it’s satisfied Singaporean entities buy its hardware on behalf of end-users in other locations, and that such deals are not used to evade the USA’s sanctions.
Nvidia is not a notably scandal-prone company, but in 2022 it did admit to having previously misrepresented the impact of cryptocurrency mining on sales of its gaming hardware. China has opened an antitrust case , and US authorities may have considered doing likewise .
Jensen Huang, however, has never presented as the kind of CEO who makes operating at the edge of the law a regular tactic. Nor does he hold sufficient Nvidia shares or voting power to unilaterally make major decisions.
This leaves the leader of the world’s top AI company appearing to have made a very human error. ®

response.stdout: Applying Monitor Design Principles In this section, we apply our monitor design principles to the medical chat and biography environments to demonstrate that our findings on the coding environment translate to other environments. We make the following monitor design modifications to improve on naive baselines: we (1) lower the threshold of the monitor to raise recall ; (2) decrease difficulty by replacing hard problems with easier ones; (3) use a more capable LLM judge monitor to increase robustness and use screening with probe monitors to prevent representation evasion. After making these changes, we observe large decreases in reward hacking and similar performance after training vs. naive intervention baselines ( Figure 11 ). Medical Chat. In the medical chat environment, patient questions are appended with leading questions that suggest a correct (50%) or incorrect (50%) diagnosis. Hackers Target OpenSSH SSHole Flaw Within Hours of Disclosure, Gain Root on Honeypot

# Hackers Target OpenSSH SSHole Flaw Within Hours of Disclosure, Gain Root on Honeypot

 Ravie Lakshmanan  Nov 06, 2026 Vulnerability / Cyber Attack

Threat actors are attempting to exploit a recently disclosed security flaw impacting OpenSSH that can enable sign-ins to accounts that have no password set, according to Previdian .

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-123158 (CVSS score: 8.1) and codenamed SSHole (or *sshole), impacts Linux systems that run OpenSSH on the musl C library with Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM) disabled, including Alpine Linux's default OpenSSH server configuration.

An unauthenticated attacker can supply an oversized password to access accounts that are deliberately configured without usable passwords, without having to steal credentials or SSH keys. The issue, discovered by security researcher Ozgun Kultekin, has been addressed in OpenSSH 10.6p2 .

The underlying issue dates back to a patch introduced in 2016 to fix a username enumeration vulnerability tracked as CVE-2016-6210 . Under specific conditions, the password-handling behavior in OpenSSH mistakenly interprets a failed password-hashing operation as successful authentication by producing the same value ("*") used to indicate that an account with password disabled at the system level.

An attacker can trigger the vulnerability to authenticate to certain password-disabled accounts using an arbitrary password between 257 and 1,024 bytes long, causing the hash attempt to fail and returning an asterisk. The sshd daemon then compares with the asterisk stored in the account's password field, leading to a successful login.

To be clear, successful exploitation requires at least one account with an asterisk (*) as its password hash. It does not allow attackers to bypass passwords on accounts with valid password hashes.

"A successful SSHole attack grants access with the compromised account's existing permissions," Safe Security said . "For enterprise, the consequences of SSHole depend on the privileges of the compromised account."

"While unauthorized SSH access is the immediate impact, attackers may also gain access to deployment credentials, application secrets, and connected infrastructure, potentially enabling lateral movement or service disruption."

Image Source: Safe Security

It's worth noting that the vulnerability does not affect Dropbear, glibc-based Linux distributions, non-Linux systems, and systems that check passwords through PAM.

Threat intelligence firm Previdian said it observed the first exploitation attempt less than nine hours after the CVE publication, adding it has confirmed successful root access on a honeypot running Alpine Linux and OpenSSH. Telemetry data shows a total of eight exploitation attempts from an IP address geolocated to Japan.

"The observed source IP, 89.116.89[.]18, used oversized passwords to bypass authentication and ran reconnaissance commands including id, uname and hostname through non-interactive SSH sessions," Ryan Dewhurst, founder and CEO of Previdian, said in a statement shared with The Hacker News.

Affected users are advised to install OpenSSH 10.6p2 or their distribution's patched package, and then restart sshd. Alpine is also recommending that users investigate "Accepted password for" log entries involvin

The FDA encourages the development of innovative, safe, and effective medical devices, including devices that incorporate artificial intelligence (AI).
The AI-Enabled Medical Device List is a resource intended to identify AI-enabled medical devices that are authorized for marketing in the United States. Digital health innovators can refer to this list to gain insights into the current device landscape and regulatory expectations, which can help foster innovation and ensure public safety. This list can also provide transparency for healthcare providers and patients to clearly identify when medical devices use AI technologies.

# Contents of the AI-Enabled Medical Devices List:

- The devices in this list have met the FDA’s applicable premarket requirements, including a focused review of the device’s overall safety and effectiveness, which includes an evaluation of study appropriateness for the device’s intended use and technological characteristics.

Instead, the list includes AI-enabled medical devices that were identified primarily based on the use of AI-related terms in the summary descriptions of their marketing authorization document and/or the device’s classification. The set of AI terms is based on the FDA Digital Health and Artificial Intelligence Glossary .

- To support transparency in the use of modern AI technologies, the FDA will explore methods to identify and tag medical devices that incorporate foundation models encompassing a wide range of AI systems, from large language models (LLMs) to multimodal architectures. This identification will help innovators, healthcare providers, and patients recognize when LLM-based functionality is present in a medical device. To facilitate the FDA’s development of methods to identify AI-enabled medical devices more easily, including identifying those devices incorporating LLM-based functionality in a future update of this list, sponsors are encouraged to include appropriate information in their public summaries.

Megaspeed is a Singapore-based AI cloud company that became one of Nvidia's largest buyers in Southeast Asia. It is now under scrutiny over possible chip smuggling to China. I didn't find the specific CNBC article in these results, so the summary below draws on other outlets.

- **Origins:** Megaspeed was created in 2023 when 7Road, a Chinese gaming and cloud computing company with ties to state-backed investors, split off its overseas operation in Singapore and renamed it Megaspeed.

HEADLINE: Microsoft says Cambodia-based Storm-3358 used ARTEX agents against Southeast Asian financial firms
PUBLISHED: November 6, 2026 (RSS pubDate Sat, 07 Nov 2026 02:44:34 +0000)
SOURCES:
Microsoft Security Blog | https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/11/06/artex-abuse-expands-as-cybercriminals-target-financial-sector/ | primary
FACTS:
- Microsoft says that "In October 2026, the financially motivated threat actor Storm-3358 began targeting organizations in the financial sector using the agentic AI offensive framework ARTEX." Microsoft Threat Intelligence describes Storm-3358 as "a Cambodia-based intrusion cluster that primarily targets financial organizations in Southeast Asia, in addition to a smaller number of large financial organizations globally."
- Microsoft says Storm-3358 used ARTEX with conventional automated tools to scan internet-connected systems, exploit flaws "including anonymous file upload and server-side request forgery (SSRF)," and install open-source RATs; it names WISP, vshell and AdaptixC2 used "for persistence and lateral movement," downloaded via netcat and curl.
- Microsoft says ARTEX "by default uses Nmap, curl, wget, Python HTTP clients, Norma SDK WebFetch, and headless Chromium through Playwright, among others," and that default user-agent strings can alert defenders even though blocking them will not stop an agent.
- Microsoft says honeypots, decoys, tarpits and "fake wins" (presenting convincing evidence the agent's objective is complete so it "stop[s] on a false success") "helped reduce the attack traffic reaching real assets and produced high-confidence, attribution-quality signal" in Microsoft's testing.
